opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed a lot, honestly. A few years ago, if you'd asked me, I would have said that for most serious ML applications, the competitive advantage came from training your own models on your own data. That was kind of the whole thesis of the MLOps world: you build the data flywheel, you collect labels, you retrain, and that loop is your moat.

What's shifted is that the general-purpose models have gotten so good, so quickly, that for the vast majority of use cases the right starting point is no longer "let's train a model." It's "let's see how far we can get with an off-the-shelf model, good prompting, retrieval, and a solid evaluation setup." And for a surprising number of problems, that gets you most of the way there, often all of it.

The way I think about it now is that training your own model has to justify itself. A few years ago it was the default. There are still good reasons to do it. Maybe you have really specialized data the foundation models have never seen. Maybe you need to run at a latency or cost point that a big hosted model can't hit. Maybe there are privacy or deployment constraints. In those cases, fine-tuning or distilling a smaller model can make a lot of sense. But I see a lot of teams reaching for training too early, before they've really exhausted what the general models can do, and before they even have a good way to measure whether their custom model is better.

The other thing I'd point out is that the moat has moved. It used to be the model weights. Now I think it's much more about everything around the model: understanding your users' problem deeply, having great evals, having the feedback loops in your product so you know when things break, and building the workflow and UX that makes the AI actually useful. Those are things a foundation model provider can't just hand you.

So my advice is usually: start general, invest heavily in evaluation, and only train when you have clear evidence that it'll move a metric you care about. That's a pretty big reversal from where I was not that long ago.

r001.rationale: It describes in-house training as the old default and the MLOps thesis, but does not identify an expectation that every business would train its own models.

r002.rationale: It says general-purpose models get teams most or all of the way on the vast majority of use cases, which communicates strong performance across most tasks.

r003.rationale: It favors starting with off-the-shelf models, but does not clearly state that they are generally more economical than developing a business’s own models.

r004.rationale: It says the moat has shifted away from model weights, but does not state that general-purpose models weakened the viability of ML infrastructure businesses built around widespread in-house training.

r005.rationale: It recommends exhausting what general-purpose models can do before training, and says to train only with clear evidence it will improve a relevant metric.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's changed a lot, honestly. When we started Gantry, and even before that when I was writing the Full Stack Deep Learning course material, the default assumption was that if you had a real business problem and some proprietary data, you were going to train a model. Maybe you'd fine-tune something off the shelf, but the core of the work was collecting data, labeling it, training, evaluating, deploying, and then iterating on that loop forever. The whole discipline of ML engineering was built around that.

What foundation models did is they flipped the default. Now the right starting point for almost everyone is: take the most capable general-purpose model you can get access to, write a prompt, and see how far that gets you. And the surprising thing, at least surprising to me a couple of years ago, is how far that actually gets you. A huge fraction of the problems people used to spin up an ML team for are now a few hundred lines of code and an API key.

So my thinking has shifted from "should you train a model" being a question about whether you have enough data, to it being a question about whether you've exhausted the cheaper options. Prompting first. Then retrieval, giving the model the right context at the right time. Then maybe fine-tuning when you have a very well-defined task and you care about cost or latency or you need behavior that's hard to specify in a prompt. Training from scratch is way down at the end of that list, and for most companies it's just never the right answer.

That said, I don't think "nobody should train models" is right either. There are two places where it still makes sense. One is when your domain is genuinely far from what the general models have seen, so the pretraining just doesn't transfer well. The other is when the economics force it, when you're running the thing at such volume that the per-token cost of a frontier model dominates your margins. In both cases though, the fundamentals haven't changed. You still need an evaluation you trust, you still need to understand where the model fails, and you still need the feedback loop from production back into development. If anything, that part got more important, because it's now the main thing differentiating a team that's good at this from a team that just has an API key.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the former default that businesses with real problems and proprietary data would train models, and connects that assumption to starting Gantry.

r002.rationale: It says general-purpose models now handle a “huge fraction” of problems that once required an ML team, indicating broad performance across business tasks.

r003.rationale: It recommends prompting and retrieval as “cheaper options” to exhaust first and says training is rarely right for most companies, conveying the general economic advantage of using available models.

r004.rationale: The candidate says foundation models changed the default and reduced the need to build ML teams, but does not state that they weakened the viability of ML infrastructure business models based on widespread in-house training.

r005.rationale: It explicitly frames the decision as whether a business has “exhausted the cheaper options,” then lists prompting and retrieval before fine-tuning or training.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s changed the starting point. In the past, if you wanted to build a machine learning product, you generally assumed you’d need to collect data and train a model for that particular problem. With general-purpose models, you can start by asking how far an existing model gets you with a good prompt and the right context.

That doesn’t mean training your own models goes away. It means you need a specific reason to do it. Maybe you have a specialized task, proprietary data, or requirements around cost and latency that a general-purpose model doesn’t meet. And even then, fine-tuning an existing model is a different decision from training one from scratch.

So I’d start with the simplest approach and build an evaluation that reflects what your users actually need. Once you can see where that approach falls short, you have a much better basis for deciding whether investing in training will help.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how businesses might approach model training, but does not identify the assumption that every business would train its own models or connect it to a generation of ML infrastructure startups.

r002.rationale: It suggests trying an existing model with a good prompt and the right context, but does not state that general-purpose language models perform well across most tasks businesses can specify within a domain.

r003.rationale: The response mentions cost as one possible reason to train, but does not claim that using commercially available general-purpose models is generally more economical.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss ML infrastructure business models or say that general-purpose models weakened their viability.

r005.rationale: The response recommends starting with an existing model and evaluating where it falls short, but does not clearly recommend exhausting the capabilities of commercially available foundation models before considering training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s changed the starting point pretty dramatically. A few years ago, if you wanted to build a product around machine learning, you generally had to collect a dataset and train a model for your particular problem. Now you can start with a general-purpose model and often get something useful just by describing what you want it to do.

That raises the bar for training your own model. I’d start with an existing model, build an evaluation that reflects what your users actually need, and see where it falls short. Then you can make a more informed decision about whether you need better prompting, better context, fine-tuning, or something more specialized.

There are still reasons to train models—cost, latency, control, or a task where you have unique data. But I think the question has shifted from ‘How do we train a model?’ to ‘What’s the simplest way to get the behavior our product needs?’

r001.rationale: The response contrasts past and present model-building practices but does not mention the expectation that every business would train its own models or connect it to ML infrastructure startups.

r002.rationale: It says a general-purpose model can often produce something useful from a description, but does not state that these models perform well across most tasks businesses can specify within a domain.

r003.rationale: The response lists cost as a reason to train a model, but does not argue that using commercially available general-purpose models is generally more economical than developing one’s own.

r004.rationale: It says general-purpose models raise the bar for training, but does not state that they weakened ML infrastructure business models premised on widespread in-house training.

r005.rationale: It recommends starting with an existing model and evaluating where it falls short, but does not clearly recommend exhausting commercially available foundation models’ capabilities before considering training a business’s own model.
